name: Stack of sheets with a focus clearing
principle: The work sits as one long pile of thin sheets seen in perspective, and the piece in focus opens a gap in the pile and turns square to the visitor while the rest stay as edges, so a whole body of work reads as one object the visitor leafs through.
freshTake: Pin one section and map page scroll to the pile, about two screens for 8-12 pieces with a light snap to each, instead of taking over the wheel or looping forever. Choose the pile from the content: a diagonal isometric pile for photographs, or for a record label or type foundry a horizontal row of sleeves or specimen cards along the lower third seen from slightly above, where the focused item stands upright at full size and the rest stay as thin spines. Fast input leans the spines sideways and they settle flat (no S-curl); one large title swaps with a vertical roll from the same centre event. A plain index of the same work sits under the section.
breaksWhen: Without WebGL or a CSS 3D fallback there is no content at all. Taking over the wheel strands keyboard and screen-reader users and anyone expecting normal scrolling. On phones the diagonal gets cramped and the focused picture is small next to its text. Mixed portrait and landscape pictures get hard cover-crops. Fewer than about 6 pieces looks thin, and a loop with few pieces repeats visibly. Trackpad momentum overshoots several sheets unless it is snapped. Long titles make the side list jump.

name: Fixed brand line over passing frames
principle: One line of type (the name, a short tagline and the navigation, or one caption per picture) stays fixed at the same height while full-bleed or column pictures slide up behind it, each seam crossing the line in turn; when every picture carries its own copy of the line inside its clipped frame, the seam slices the old words off and the new ones are already standing, so the brand or the caption reads as a constant the world moves past.
freshTake: For a restaurant, two or three full-bleed frames (the room, a dish, hands at work), each with a slight in-frame drift, scroll up behind one line holding the name, a short tagline and three links, fixed at about 62% of the screen height rather than dead centre. The line's colour flips between ground and ink exactly where each seam passes behind it (two clipped copies, one per frame), with no drop shadow, so choose frames whose band at that height is calm. When the last frame leaves, the line rides away with it and uncovers a compact header waiting underneath. On phones the line stays sticky at the same height with no drift.
breaksWhen: Busy or high-contrast pictures behind the line hurt legibility, and a drop shadow to rescue it breaks the house style. A long tagline or many links wrap and break the single line. A whole-line colour switch flips mid-letter at the seam; it needs a clip per frame. More than three frames make the opening drag.

name: Object lands on the last line
principle: Over the last screens of the page a rendered object comes down from above with uneven pacing, a slow creep for half the scroll and most of its frames at the end, and sets down exactly on the closing statement, so the page ends on the product arriving.
freshTake: For a furniture maker, a single chair is lowered from above by an off-screen hand over the last two screens of normal scroll and set down exactly on the baseline of one large sentence-case line in ink: Made to be sat in for forty years. Frames follow the scroll unevenly: the first half of the scroll plays about 10% of the frames and the last third plays most of them, smoothed so it creeps and then settles. Flat ground and solid type, with no outline wordmark, glow or shimmer. On phones play a shorter, half-resolution sequence.
breaksWhen: Needs a high-quality render or locked-off film of the object arriving and coming to rest, 60-100 frames on a matching or transparent ground; a moving camera will not sit on the page. Under about 50 frames the fast final stretch stutters. A closing section shorter than about 1.5 screens squashes the creep-then-drop into a jump. An outline wordmark, a gradient fade, soft glows or a wall of partner logos break house rules.

name: Parked object marks the row beneath it
principle: An object arrives, parks in a fixed slot on screen and marks each row of a list as it slides underneath, then leaves at the end and comes back turned round when the visitor scrolls up, so a plain schedule reads as if the object is travelling through it.
freshTake: For a sailing regatta, a top-down photographed hull glides in from the left and moors at the left third while full-width rows pass on the right with each race date in large numerals; a row's date turns to the accent as it passes the bow and back to ink after. At the end of the list the hull sails off to the right, and if the visitor scrolls back it returns from the right with its bow turned. Never park the object inside the section title, and keep the row text clear of it.
breaksWhen: Short lists make it park and leave almost at once; it needs 6-12 rows. On phones the object covers the text it should mark unless it shrinks to the edge. Very fast scrolling makes the highlights flicker. It feels like a gimmick if the object has nothing to do with the list.

name: Breathing band of pictures
principle: A looping chain of pictures standing on one baseline moves along a line where each one's size comes from a function of its position (a bell curve, or a ramp that climbs toward one edge) and the shift is multiplied by the size so neighbours always stay touching, so items are born as slivers, swell as they travel along the line and shrink or leave, and the whole band breathes as the scroll pushes it.
freshTake: Run a straight horizontal band of 5-7 book covers, products or portraits along the baseline of a typographic opening on a flat ground, with no diagonal staircase. The scroll alone drives it, with no idle drift: one screen of hold moves it most of a lap. The centre item is always the largest, and its title stands in large set type above it, swapping as the next item takes the centre. Each picture zooms slightly inside its frame as the frame narrows. On phones run it as a vertical column of 3-5 tiles down one side, each swelling as it passes the middle of the screen.
breaksWhen: On phones the end frames turn hair-thin and only about three pictures read. Subjects near the edges are lost to the crop and zoom. Fewer than four pictures repeat visibly in the loop. An endless idle drift ignores reduced motion and never lets the page rest. A headline or button placed where the band is largest fights it.

name: Panels cross a held ground
principle: On a held stage the ground is swapped in uneven bands, a few panels then travel across it while it stays perfectly still, and the last panel's exit drags the ground away to uncover the next one, so the content seems to move through a place rather than over a page.
freshTake: For a winery's three estates, hold a flat field of the page's ground with the region name set large, then wipe it to a vineyard photograph in five horizontal bands that close from the top down. Three plain square estate panels with hard edges and no frame then rise up the screen in a column while the photograph holds, each with a photo, the estate name and one line. As the last panel leaves at the top it pulls the photograph up with it and uncovers a cellar photograph with one closing line. Use one ink colour for all type and about two screens of hold. On phones the panels go full width and the band wipe uses three bands.
breaksWhen: Held much past two screens it drags; with thin panels even four feel endless, and more than five panels make it longer still. The band wipe only reads when the two grounds differ strongly. Light type over photographs needs grounds that stay calm behind it. Small bracketed uppercase coordinates and tinted card frames break house rules. Visitors who want one item have to pass all of them.

name: Panels re-proportion as they arrive
principle: Panels slide in over a held opening and each one changes its own inner split as it travels into place, arriving as half picture and half type and settling as mostly picture with its name re-set below, so every item visibly comes into focus rather than just passing by.
freshTake: Hold a typographic opening (one statement on the flat ground, no darkened photo) and let four or five tall panels slide in from the right over it, about half a screen of scroll each. Each panel is one picture over a band of the page's own ground. It arrives split 50/50, and as it reaches its slot the picture grows to about 70% and pushes the band down, so the name re-sets from one line onto two in large type with a hard cut, no blur. All panels share one ground and one ink; only the pictures tell them apart. Suits a publisher's imprints, a school's programmes or a developer's buildings. On phones the panels stack vertically without a pin, and each re-proportions as it crosses the middle of the screen.
breaksWhen: Fewer than four panels ends before the change of ratio is noticed, and more than six makes a long hold. Short or wide screens squash the picture part if the band has a fixed height. Long names overflow the band. Similar photos blur together. Animating grid rows forces layout every frame and stutters on heavy pages, so animate with transforms or clips. A colour per panel breaks the one-accent rule.

name: Queue steps forward as the front leaves
principle: A held stack or row shows one item at the front with the rest waiting behind, and each scroll beat sends the front item off the stage while the whole queue advances one notch with a small springy overshoot, so a list of services or products is met one at a time with a physical rhythm.
freshTake: Four to six items at about half a screen of scroll each, so the hold stays at two screens. Either tall portrait photographs, each with its one- or two-word name set on the ground below the picture (no gradient band over the photo), or, with no pictures, a row of tall flat panels alternating ground and ink with the item's name set large and vertical. The front item leaves by dropping straight down below the fold with no random tilt, and the queue slides one step toward the front with a small overshoot. The opposite column swaps a one-line summary in step with each beat, and the last item stays as the section releases, its name a link to the full list. On phones the queue stacks vertically in square crops and advances upward. Variant on a shallow diagonal in perspective: the next item rises nearer at one corner and earlier ones recede smaller toward the other; each item behind the front one trails the move by about 60 ms so the row ripples, and the side text and count cut out and back in on hard line masks only once the row has come to rest.
breaksWhen: Fewer than four items leave the hold empty and more than eight make it drag; anything past two screens of hold is too long. A random tilt can swing a big card through the fixed nav on short screens. Long names wrap over the picture. Weak or similar photos make it read as a generic stacked-cards widget, and rounded cards with shadows, a gradient behind the labels or a drawn squiggle behind the deck break the house style.

name: Speed-bent ribbon of work
principle: A row of work pictures stands on one shared curved surface in 3D, near ones looming and far ones receding, and scroll speed deepens the curve and leans its ends before it settles back, so the whole body of work reads as one flexible object that the visitor's own pace bends. The same speed-bend can be laid on a whole page or one big element, a list of huge names or one headline included: edges pinned or each line tipping about its own edge, the middle lagging, leaning and stretching in proportion to the speed, then easing back to a flat, clean setting as soon as the scroll stops.
freshTake: For a record shop's new releases, stand square sleeves on a shallow concave bowl seen a little from above, on a warm paper ground with no drawn floor and no reflection. Pin the section for about two screens and map page scroll to the row, with no wheel takeover and no drag; scroll speed makes the leading sleeves lean back like records flipped in a crate and the far end lift, then everything settles. Titles are printed on the same curve. A plain list of the releases sits under the section, and on phones the row becomes a vertical stack that bows with speed.
breaksWhen: Fewer than about 6 items makes the row thin and any loop repeat visibly. Phones lose the curve and need the vertical fallback. Taking over the wheel with no native scroll strands keyboard and screen-reader users, so the work must also exist as plain HTML. Many video textures plus a full-screen GL canvas strain weak GPUs. Long titles on the far side shrink with perspective. Pushing the lean too far moves drawn cards off their DOM hit areas. Mouse drag and fling would make it a drag rail.

name: Hero object shrinks into the first card
principle: The object that held the hero is measured onto the exact on-screen rectangle of the first content card and shrinks into it under the scroll, so the object becomes that card, and the remaining cards then slide in beside it on the same held stage, so the page moves from showing the product to explaining it without a cut.
freshTake: For a coffee roaster: a full-bleed photograph of one sack of green beans holds the hero. Under the scroll it shrinks onto the exact rectangle of the first origin card, measured from the live card and remeasured on resize, while its crop tightens to the card's shape; instead of a 3D shatter the photograph is cut into a 6 by 4 grid of tiles that settle into the rectangle with a short stagger. Four more origins then slide in from the right as the visitor keeps scrolling down, never by dragging, each one a photograph with its name and three short lines set beneath it on the page ground: no panel fill, no glow, square corners.
breaksWhen: Packed into a tiny stretch of scroll, a normal flick skips the whole change. If the target is not remeasured on resize and font load, the object lands beside the card instead of on it. Card text drawn in WebGL is not selectable or readable by screen readers; keep it in the DOM. On phones a sideways deck moved by vertical scroll confuses people who try to swipe sideways, and it must never become draggable (house ban). More than about five cards makes the sideways travel drag on.

name: Chapter shrinks into the overview, the next one opens
principle: The full-screen chapter the visitor is in shrinks back into its place among all the chapters, the whole set moves to bring the next one forward, and that one grows back to fill the screen, so every change of chapter briefly shows the map of the whole.
freshTake: For a design school's six departments, the departments lie as a flat contact sheet of full-bleed crops separated by thin gutters of the page ground, with no frames, tilt or rounded corners. The open department, full screen with its one-line name, shrinks back into its place until about nine crops show, the view glides one place across the sheet, and the next department grows back to full screen, all on real page scroll in a pinned section of about half a screen per department, snapping on each. The name changes as a plain text swap.
breaksWhen: Taking over the wheel kills page scroll and long-form content; trackpads start a momentum spin on the smallest gesture, and touch gets no swipe. Fewer than four chapters make no overview to read, and past eight the set crowds. Every chapter has to be designed twice, as a full screen and as a small crop, and needs its own loop or interaction or the settled state goes dead. Adding real perspective changes the look, so a rebuild must choose it deliberately.

name: Turning object becomes the next variant
principle: One object turns slowly at the centre of a held stage and, as the scroll advances, changes mid-turn into the next variant of itself while a short list of their names beside it lights one at a time, so a range (materials, flavours, finishes) reads as one thing transforming rather than a row of products.
freshTake: For a perfumer, one bottle seen straight on turns a quarter turn per scent while the liquid inside shifts to the next scent's tone, four scents in about two screens. The scent names stand as a large list on the left in the ink with the current one in the accent and a slight weight change, and the ground never changes. No ring of ticks or dial around the bottle and no small code columns.
breaksWhen: Needs a custom render that both turns and morphs; with plain photos it becomes a slideshow. More than about six variants makes each step too short to read. Hundreds of frames are heavy where WebCodecs is missing. On phones the list has to move under the object. A coloured ground breaks a white-canvas render unless the frames carry transparency.

name: Camera climbs away from a locked subject
principle: Looking straight down on one subject at work, the scroll lifts the camera until the subject is a sliver in its wide ground while it stays centred and its live surroundings stay locked to it, the message gathers in toward its line, and a closing layer slides in from the edges to end the climb, so scale and reach are felt rather than stated.
freshTake: For a farming co-operative, start overhead on one tractor cutting a fresh strip through a field; the scroll lifts the view until the field becomes a patchwork of plots and the tractor a dot, while the co-op's five commitments slide in from both sides onto the tractor's row line at different speeds. The climb ends when flat sheets of the page ground slide in from the four edges and close the view. One very large aerial photograph scaled in step with the tractor cut-out; no haze, no blur.
breaksWhen: The overhead photograph must stay sharp at the closest zoom and its ground must hold at both scales. Without a live ground (water that moves, a field in wind) the subject slides over a still photo and looks pasted on. Long reasons collide with the subject's line in the middle. Photographic closing layers shown at 8x need huge files. A dimming layer or a blur-in headline is a soft effect and goes.

name: Split halves wipe in opposite directions
principle: On a held stage each chapter is split into two halves, and every change wipes the next chapter in on the left half from one edge and on the right half from the opposite edge, the pictures sliding inside their wipes and one big headline set as two lines with the break on the join, a whole line riding each half, so a run of projects turns over like two shutters passing each other and every rest is a whole poster.
freshTake: For a furniture maker's three collections, turn it a quarter turn: the stage is a top half and a bottom half on one flat ground. Each collection's top half slides in from the right while its bottom half slides in from the left, so two vertical seams pass each other, and the collection name is set as two huge lines with the line break exactly on the horizontal join, one line riding each half, all in the one ink. Each half carries one photograph (a chair above, its joint in close-up below) that trails its seam by about 20% and catches up. Each change takes about three quarters of a screen and is followed by a short rest so the poster is whole, so the three collections hold for about two screens before the stage lets go into ordinary scroll. No colour per collection and no counter at the join; the accent only on the single link under the name.
breaksWhen: Long headline words overflow a half, and the two copies of the headline must break their lines identically or the join tears. Every chapter needs two crops that work as halves, or a half looks padded. Many pictures or clips on one stage get heavy, so use stills or very short loops. Fewer than three chapters and the move is over before it reads. Without smooth scrolling the scrub looks steppy. A colour per project breaks the one ground, one ink, one accent rule. A fixed stage that never ends leaves nowhere for the footer, so it must release into ordinary scroll.

name: Wavefront from the point of action uncovers the picture
principle: A picture is uncovered by one wavefront that spreads from a meaningful point (the spot just tapped, the option chosen, the corner nearest the heading) and visibly disturbs the picture as it passes before leaving it still and sharp, so the picture seems set off by something rather than faded or wiped in.
freshTake: For a running-shoe maker: one full-width photograph of the shoe shot on a flat, plain ground sits under the section heading, covered at first by the page ground. When the band is half in view, one hard-edged ring spreads from the point directly under the heading's last word; just inside the ring the photograph is pushed outward in square blocks along three stepped bands, behind it the picture is still and sharp, ahead of it the flat colour holds, about 1.4 s in all, then the blocks snap to zero. No refraction, no soft light bands, no glow; on phones the band stays full width so the ring has room to travel.
breaksWhen: Busy photographic grounds turn the disturbance into a smear, so the subject needs a flat ground. A fast scroller lets the reveal play off-screen. A ring from an arbitrary centre reads as a generic transition; the origin has to mean something. Each WebGL canvas costs a context and a texture, so several on a page need a 2D or CSS fallback. Small cards cramp the rings on a phone. A cut-out whose ground differs from the cover colour leaves a visible rectangle when it settles.

name: Type sets like wet ink
principle: Display type exists first as swollen, merged ink blobs and sharpens into clean letters line by line as it reaches its place on screen, because a blur is pushed through a hard alpha threshold that relaxes as the blur clears, so words seem to set like wet ink rather than fade in.
freshTake: For a mineral-water brand's manifesto, set four short lines of a heavy round grotesk in one ink on a flat chalk ground, one line per screen of native scroll. Each line condenses out of chunky blobs as it rises from the lower third to the centre, and stays crisp once set, with the blur at 8px at most, so the reader sets the pace line by line; the last line stays crisp with the one button under it. Nothing else on the page melts: every other heading cuts or slides plainly, no accent colour in the lines, no paragraph or drawings around them.
breaksWhen: Thin, light or serif faces lose their hairlines in the threshold and settle looking bolder than set. Over photographs or busy grounds the blobs read as dirt. One SVG filter per line is costly: more than four or five moving at once stutters on phones and in some browsers, so attach the filter only while a line moves and remove it at rest. Fonts must load before the lines are split. Reduced motion needs a plain cut to crisp type. Used on every heading of a page it becomes a tic.

name: Folded document opens into the page
principle: One document the product makes (an invoice, a contract, an invitation) arrives folded, rises into place and opens panel by panel on its hinges until it lies flat and turns into the live, readable version, so the visitor is handed the product's output as a thing rather than shown a screenshot of it.
freshTake: For billing software, a gate-folded invoice: the closed card is a narrow centre panel (logo, invoice number, amount due) standing on the flat ground. When the section enters, the two side wings swing open on their vertical hinges, the right one 80 ms after the left, over 0.9 s on a slow-start, quick-settle curve, showing the line items on one wing and the due date with the Pay button on the other. Depth comes only from flat tone: each wing's back is a darker flat tint of the ground and its face is paper, so the tone flips at the halfway point; no line at the hinges, no shadow, no gradient, no bowing. When both wings land, the 3D rig is swapped for the real DOM invoice, which can grow downward with more rows. On phones the wings become top and bottom flaps; reduced motion shows the open invoice.
breaksWhen: The rig rests on strips of fixed height, so long or translated copy, long words or a narrow phone reflow and clip inside a strip or jump at the hand-over to the flat version. Played on load it hides the readable content for over three seconds on every visit. Some browsers, older mobile ones most, render hidden backfaces and nested 3D unreliably, so seams can flicker at the hinges. A soft drop shadow for depth is banned at rest; depth comes from flat tone. A product with no document-shaped output has nothing honest to fold.

name: A hand dealt one card per beat
principle: Cards are dealt one at a time onto a pile, each arriving turned (tilted in the plane, or swung in from edge-on) and settling at its own small angle on top of the last, either fanned along a huge arc or levelled almost flat, while a title holds beside or beneath them, so a short set of items is laid down like a hand of cards being played.
freshTake: For a type foundry's four weights: tall paper strips hang from the top edge of the screen like pendants on an arc whose centre sits far above the viewport, and each beat swings a new strip in from the left in a hard 150 ms snap with no spring, the set re-centring as it lands. Strips alternate ground and ink, told apart by colour alone with no edge line or shadow, and each carries its weight's name set in that weight, large enough to read on the covered strips. Four strips at about half a screen each, and the section releases on the full set.
breaksWhen: The fan needs about 940 px of width for four cards; phones need a vertical fan or a plain stack. More than five cards spread past a laptop screen. Stepping relative to the last step leaves cards missing after a reload mid-pin or a hard fling; set every card from the current step. Body text on covered cards is unreadable, so only the top card is really read. A colour per card breaks the house palette, overlapping cards alternate ground and ink rather than take an edge line or a shadow, and big 1-2-3-4 numerals on the cards are banned numbering.

name: Scenes hand over by zooming through each other
principle: On a fixed stage each full-screen scene leaves by growing past the viewer and fading while the next one settles from oversized to fit, each carrying one statement that rises in and out with it, so several chapters pass as one forward drift with no section ever scrolling by.
freshTake: For a soil-science lab: three still photographs (a field from above, a core sample, a hand in the soil) untouched, or all in greyscale as the page's one treatment. On one scrubbed timeline over two screens, the outgoing plate grows to 1.4x and fades while the incoming plate settles from 1.5x to 1; each plate carries one short line in the display face, two lines at most and left-aligned, that rises 60px in and out with it. Nothing lies over the plates as they hand over, no wash and no frosted layer, and the last plate carries one large accent figure that counts up in place of tooltip dots. A paper-coloured section then slides up over the stage.
breaksWhen: Plates must match in grade and brightness or the dissolve reads as a cut. Three looping videos at once are heavy and can be blocked from autoplay, so stills are the default. Text over pictures loses contrast on pale areas unless the plate is darkened flat. Timing set in fixed pixels drifts with window height, so key it to the held section. Anchor jumps land mid-dissolve. Phones need portrait crops.

name: Facts rise through a fixed window of light
principle: A tall object with its facts printed down its face moves up in steps through one fixed window that is clear inside and dimmed outside, so exactly one fact is legible at a time and the visitor reads the object itself instead of a list beside it.
freshTake: For an olive-oil producer: a flat photograph of the bottle's long back label stands tall on the paper ground. A fixed hard-edged rectangular window across the middle of the screen shows the label at full strength inside and at 40% outside. In four scroll steps the label slides up so one claim at a time sits in the window (pressed within six hours, one estate, harvest date on every bottle, unfiltered), and each claim is set large in the body face beside it with a hard cut, the accent used only for the active claim. No glow, no blur, no 3D.
breaksWhen: The window and the printed facts are aligned by eye for one aspect ratio; other screens need them measured. Text inside a picture is invisible to search and screen readers, so each fact also stands as page text. Fewer than three facts makes the move thin; more than five needs a long travel. A low-resolution label goes soft at the crop. Portrait phones need the window and its text stacked.

name: Curved carousel flattened by the lens
principle: Pictures stand bent round a large drum seen through a wide lens, the scroll turns the drum to bring one to the front, and then the camera backs away while the lens lengthens, so the front picture loses its curve and grows into one flat full-width picture as its neighbours leave the frame, and a 3D carousel becomes an editorial spread through optics alone. Run backwards it reveals a set: a full-frame clip turns out to be the front panel of a ring standing round the visitor, its neighbours light up outward from it in pairs, and the camera backs out while the ring swings and tilts until the whole drum of moving pictures hangs small in the frame.
freshTake: For a fashion house's five looks: five portrait photographs stand round a drum about its vertical axis in CSS 3D, seen through a short perspective of about 500 px so the curve is plain, and the scroll turns the drum sideways until the chosen look stands in front. Over the next screen the perspective rises to about 6000 px while the stage scales up, so the front look loses its bend and grows into one flat full-height column in the centre third as its neighbours leave the frame, and its name is set very large beside it in one flat ink. The section ends on that still spread. Flat saturated ground, no counter ring, no shader, no clip-path wipes.
breaksWhen: Tuned to a fixed count: the turn is sized so the chosen picture lands in front, so adding one throws it off-centre. The bend distorts text printed in pictures. The final flat picture shows only the middle of each frame, so subjects near its edges are cut. On phones the bent pictures shrink to strips. Keyboard and reduced-motion visitors need a plain stack, and the scroll length must be re-measured once the 3D layer has loaded. Turned about a horizontal axis like a card file it becomes the overused scroll-turned drum, so the drum turns sideways.

name: Picture ribbon wound past giant type
principle: A continuous strip of pictures bends along a 3D curve like cloth round a spool, swinging from face-on to edge-on as it travels past oversized words that slide the other way, and when the strip runs out some of its pictures fly in from the edges and land as a tidy grid with a short damped ripple, so a body of work passes as one moving object and then sits still to be read.
freshTake: For a knitwear label: eight portrait photographs of garments ride a river-bend S curve instead of a spiral, past one oversized single word that the strip wipes away from left to right as it passes. When the strip has gone, four of the photographs fly into a 4 by 1 contact row along the bottom with a short damped ripple while the word sets itself again in the space above, in the ink. Flat warm-white ground, ink type, no guide lines, no shadows, and a plain CSS 3D fallback of eight cards where WebGL is missing.
breaksWhen: Fine detail and text inside the pictures are unreadable while bent and moving. Fewer than six distinct pictures leaves repeats in the grid. The pictures live only in the canvas, so links and alt text need a DOM copy. Phones need a shorter hold and a two-column grid. The held section must start exactly at the top, so the section before it has to end cleanly. Decorative guide hairlines add nothing and go; the giant words stay plain type with the pictures passing in front, never set inside the headline.

name: Wall of cards folds edge-on into one sliver
principle: A set of same-ratio pictures opens from one card into a wide fanned wall stepped back in depth, holds while the visitor reads, then every card turns edge-on and slides to the centre line until the whole wall is a single thin sliver, and that sliver opens as the band into the next scene, so a collection is shown, folded away and turned into the doorway onward in one object.
freshTake: For a ceramics shop: fourteen square photographs of single pieces on one plain bone backdrop. One photograph sits alone at the centre, and the scroll fans it out into a straight perspective corridor of tiles stepped back in depth on either side, the two nearest held large and sharp for half a screen. Then the tiles flick edge-on one after another from the outside in, like pages turning, and close onto the centre line as one ink-thin spine, which widens into a full-width band holding the photograph of the shop's room, where the two-line headline is set for the first time. One ground, one ink, no colour flood, no labels or markers round the wall.
breaksWhen: Under about eight cards the wall looks thin, and busy pictures blur together where they overlap, so each needs one flat backdrop. Twelve to sixteen 3D-transformed layers under a perspective of about 500 px are fine on desktop but heavy on weak phones, and edge-on cards with too short a perspective read as distortion. Phones need a fan of five or a plain stacked grid, never a drag rail. A ground that floods with a second colour, or tiny mono labels round the wall, break the house rules. The fold only pays off if the next scene really opens from a band.

name: Scroll trades weight between headline and text
principle: On a held stage the scroll drives a variable font's weight axis, so one block of type thins from its heaviest cut to a hairline while another thickens the opposite way, and the moment where the two cross becomes the turn of the statement, so the type itself is the thing that changes rather than anything around it.
freshTake: For a bicycle-frame builder: a flat bone ground, one ink, one accent. Two left-aligned lines in a variable grotesque, 'Built heavy.' over 'Ridden light.', at about 9vw on a held stage for about one and a half screens. The scroll drives the first line from weight 100 up to 900 and the second from 900 down to 100, so each line only becomes its own word at the end; at the crossing, both at 500, ground and ink swap in one cut, with no accent in the lines. No film behind, no list of weight names, no number readout, nothing else on the stage.
breaksWhen: A static font, or a variable font with a narrow range (200 to 700 reads timid), cannot do it. Thinner letters are narrower and heavier ones wider, so long words or narrow phones re-wrap mid-sweep and the block jumps; keep short lines that fit at the heaviest weight, left-aligned or in a fixed box. Rewriting the weight of long copy on every scroll tick forces relayout that stutters on weak phones. Weight names, if shown, stay sentence case at normal size. Two screens with one statement frustrate visitors who want to move on. Reduced motion jumps to a middle weight.

name: Each arrival pushes the deck back a rung
principle: Each new item slides up into the front slot of a deck seen in depth while every item already there steps one rung back, smaller and higher, and the oldest fades out, so a list is laid down like records dropped into a crate and one whole item always rests in front.
freshTake: For a design studio's six services, pin one section. Each service is a full-width flat poster card carrying one huge word at its top edge and two lines of copy under it, the cards alternating the page's ground and ink so neighbouring rungs separate without a third colour. The next card slides up flat from below the fold into the front slot while every card already in the deck steps one rung back and up, shrinking to about 0.84 and then 0.72, toward a vanishing point at the upper right so the deck recedes on a diagonal; only three rungs show and the fourth fades as it goes, so the word on each back card's top strip still names it. About a third of a screen of scroll per card, with a soft settle so one card always rests in front. When the deck rests, one large sentence-case line under it cuts (no fade) to the front card's summary, and the single accent marks only the front card's link. After the sixth card the pin lets go into ordinary scroll: no loop, no counter.
breaksWhen: Back items show only a top strip, so items that look alike (similar covers, same ground) turn the rungs to mush; separate them by alternating ground and ink or by a word set at the top edge, never by a colour per item. Short or landscape windows squeeze the stack into the top half when the front item is tall. Fewer than about five items shows the end too soon; more than eight makes a long hold. An endless wrapping deck hides the footer and fights find, keyboard paging and screen readers, so release after one pass. An entrance that opens from a slit is the overused clip-path shutter, and a backdrop blur on the receding items is glass; use scale and fade only. Sticky stacking breaks under any ancestor with overflow hidden. Phones need a shallower depth and the whole front item in view.

name: World develops around the camera
principle: A scroll-scrubbed camera travels through a sparse world of flat cut-outs set at depth, and nothing is there until the camera comes near: each piece develops out of the blank ground as it enters a set range and steps back into the ground once passed, so the journey reads as islands of the subject materialising out of an empty page.
freshTake: For an antique-furniture dealer: eight photographed cut-outs of pieces (a chair, a chest, a clock, a lamp) placed at different depths and sideways offsets in a CSS 3D stage on one flat paper ground, and one scroll-scrubbed move over two screens that slides the perspective origin sideways and translates the stage in depth. Each piece is a flat silhouette in the ground colour until it comes within a set depth, then steps to full colour in three hard steps, and steps back to the ground colour once passed; the far distance is empty paper. One large sentence sits bottom left and changes once at the midpoint. No haze, no ragged paint edge, no shadow under the pieces.
breaksWhen: With fewer than about six pieces the world feels empty rather than curated. Reveals on a clock fall behind a fast scroller; tie each reveal to the camera's distance, not to time. Distance haze, soft ground shadows and a gradient backdrop are all banned, so depth must come from stepped flat colour. A slowed wheel makes the section feel stuck; keep native scroll speed. Phones and weak GPUs struggle with a full 3D scene and a depth fog pass; a CSS 3D stack is lighter. Reduced motion needs a still arrangement.

name: View travels down a tall turning object
principle: One tall object stays in frame while the scroll turns it once on its axis and slides the view down its height from top to foot, and short statements are handed off as the view passes the parts they name, one set behind the object and the next in front of it, so the visitor reads the thing from top to bottom the way they would look it over in person.
freshTake: For a ceramicist: a tall vase shot as a 72-frame turntable on the paper ground, drawn to a canvas with a crop about 40% of the vase's height that travels from lip to foot as the frames advance over two screens. Three short statements set left-aligned in the left third stand beside the part they talk about (lip, body, foot), each swapped with a hard line mask, the first behind the vase's silhouette and the next in front of it. When the crop reaches the foot the ground flips from paper to ink in one step as the paragraph arrives. No soft dissolve of the base, no shadow, no 3D engine.
breaksWhen: A poor scan or flat lighting kills it; the object must hold up close all the way down. A full-screen model with soft shadows is heavy on mid and low phones. If the scene fails to mount, statements that wait on it must not stay hidden; give the section a still and visible text. Text states flipped by callbacks land wrong on a fast flick or an anchor jump, so derive them from progress. A soft dissolve of the object into the ground is a gradient and is banned; end on a hard crop. Long statements at display size wrap into too many lines.

name: Camera runs down a corridor whose walls are the page's own words
principle: The camera glides down a rectangular corridor whose floor and side walls (and optionally its ceiling) are set in rows of the page's own short words, perspective shrinking the rows toward a far opening, so a short list of what the business does becomes a place the visitor passes through and the far end hands over to the next section.
freshTake: Build the corridor in CSS 3D (perspective on a pinned stage, a preserve-3d corridor) with a floor and two side walls and no ceiling, so the ground colour stays open above like sky. Each wall is a column of rows set in the single ink: for a bakery the left wall reads 'flour, water, salt, time', the right wall 'mixed at four, baked by six', the floor 'open at seven', the rows shrinking by perspective alone. Scrub a translateZ across about two pinned screens on native scroll, no wheel hijack. At the far end the corridor opens onto a flat panel in the ground colour that carries the next section's headline, so leaving the corridor is the hand-over to the next section. On portrait screens drop the side walls and run the sentences down the floor only.
breaksWhen: Words longer than about ten letters stop fitting across the floor at a size that reads; fewer than three items leaves a wall empty and more than five needs a different shape. Needs a very heavy condensed face so cropped letters still read, and 3D transforms. A visitor who flicks fast crosses the whole corridor in one movement unless it is scrubbed on native scroll. On portrait phones the side walls shrink to slivers, so keep the floor only. A second accent on the floor, gradient fades on the walls' ends and monospace hint lines break house bans; keep one ground, one ink, one accent and plain words.

name: Pinned set cycles by pose, no card ever leaves
principle: On a held stage a small set of cards is posed by its distance from the active one (the front card at full size, its neighbours a step smaller beside or behind it), and the scroll steps the active index (or the pointer's position picks it) so the whole set cycles: the front card steps aside, the next comes forward and the one at the far end wraps round to the other side, while a name or list row beside the set changes in the same step.
freshTake: For a hotel's three room types: a pinned stage with three tall photographs in a row on one paper ground, the active one at full height in the centre and its two neighbours at 82% tucked behind it on either side, no tilt. Each step moves the centre photograph to the left slot, the right one to the centre and the left one round behind to the right, in a 0.6s ease with a hard stop. The room's name, set huge above the row, changes with a hard cut on the same step. A list of the three room names runs under the row and the active name takes the accent. No ring, no tag pills, no tilt, nothing below 80% scale. About 0.7 of a screen per room, and the stage lets go with the last room centred.
breaksWhen: Needs about three to six cards: with exactly three the wrap is obvious and more than three needs more poses than left and right. Cards of unequal ratio or busy backgrounds ruin the rhythm. The visitor cannot jump to item three without passing two, the first tenth of the run changes nothing so a heading must carry it, and poses set by an index class animate on a timer, so a fast scroller sees lag. Four cards cost about five screens. On phones the stage becomes a swipe strip or a vertical stack with the neighbours reduced to edges. A counter ring, orbiting hairlines, tag pills and uppercase statements are banned; a filling ring is a scroll-progress bar too, so let the changing name carry the step.

name: Statements pull into focus under the scroll
principle: On a held stage short statements arrive by focus rather than by movement: each word or line comes in oversized, soft and faint and sharpens into place under one scrubbed value a little behind the reader, then leaves the same way or is pushed out while the next statement, or a paragraph drifting up through it, takes over, so a run of statements plays as a relay of focus pulls.
freshTake: For a research lab's three findings: three statements of five to eight words in a heavy grotesque, ink on a flat paper ground, left-aligned at one height on a stage held for two screens. Each word, not each letter, comes in from 125 percent scale and a 6 px blur to sharp over its own slice of the scroll, the blur gone in the first third of its travel; once a statement is sharp, its one-sentence explanation in the body face rises up through and past it at 1.4 times the scroll speed, and the statement then leaves by focus in reverse while the next arrives. No accent word in a statement, no picture behind, and on touch the blur is dropped for a plain opacity rise.
breaksWhen: Animated blur on dozens of split letters is costly on low-end phones, so split by word and drop the blur on touch. A fast scroll swaps statements before they are read unless each rests sharp for a stretch. Text over a busy picture or video loses contrast mid-pull, so keep the ground flat. A paragraph crossing the statement hurts legibility for a moment and needs short text. Screen readers get split letters unless the sentence sits whole in an aria-label. More than two screens of hold feel stuck if nothing else happens on the stage.

name: Parts leave the assembly and the total counts down with them
principle: On one scrubbed timeline an assembled object pulls apart along one axis into its separate parts, each by a different distance, and the parts are read one at a time: at each stop one part stands alone beside its name and one fact while the rest step back, or, for a claim of lightness, modularity or price, each part carries its own number and the optional ones turn edge-on and shrink away while a total counts down to the core that is left; scrolling back puts it together again, so the visitor learns what the thing is made of by taking it apart.
freshTake: A plan builder for a modular sofa with no WebGL: eight flat photo cut-outs of modules sit in a CSS 3D row with perspective. Scroll pulls them apart sideways and in depth on a small stagger and a price in plain body type rises beside each. Then the optional modules turn edge-on and vanish one by one while the total at top right counts down from the full set to the two-seat core, which stays. Show the total large beside a plain itemised list where each removed line's price counts to zero and the line dims. Flat warm ground, no monospace, no ring, no glow, no bars.
breaksWhen: Needs an object already split into separately addressable parts and real numbers on each, otherwise the countdown is decoration. A spin plus a dozen labels is cluttered at phone width, so cut the label count. Labels re-projected from 3D can overlap while parts cross. If the data changes, the shrink order and the legend must be rebuilt by hand. Heavy composer rendering stutters on weak GPUs.

name: Two objects slide in from the edges and meet under the closing line
principle: In the closing screen two mirrored objects slide in from opposite screen edges on one scroll value while a giant closing line stands whole and a button grows from nothing, and the objects touch under it, so the page ends on a gesture of arrival rather than a form.
freshTake: DOM only: two photographed glasses as cut-outs slide in from the left and right edges with transform only, the toast headline stands whole in the ink, the glasses touch at the end of the hold, and the button is a plain rectangle that scales from 0.4 to 1. No icons, no mouse parallax.
breaksWhen: Needs art that reads as two things meeting (two arms, two glasses, two hands). The objects must be shot at the same scale as the words, so on tall phones they get tiny and the words stack. A burst of confetti where they meet is decorative particles and is banned. A link drawn in a GL scene needs a real anchor for keyboard and screen readers.

name: Names turn on the rim of a huge wheel
principle: A column of short names curves along the rim of a wheel far larger than the screen, each name tilted along its spoke, and one scrubbed number turns the wheel through a little CSS trigonometry, so each name lights as it passes the middle of the arc.
freshTake: For a restaurant's ten dishes (or ten talks, ten rooms): put the hub below the bottom centre of the screen so the names fan across the upper half like a dial, each word rotated about its inner end and set in a serif at about 6vw. One scrubbed number turns the dial; the dish crossing twelve o'clock takes the accent, the others stay in the muted ink, and that dish's two-line description is set in plain text under the dial. One ground, one ink, one accent, no video behind it. On a phone the radius shrinks and only five names are in view at once.
breaksWhen: Names over about 14 characters run into whatever sits beside the arc, and fewer than seven names leave the rim half empty. cos() and sin() inside calc() need browsers from about 2023. Below about 1200 px the arc needs its own smaller radius and fewer visible names. The unlit names stay in the muted ink, never faded, so they still read. Letting a glowing video sit behind the arc turns the ground into a gradient; build it on one flat ground.

name: Section seam sinks into a pocket that gathers the scattered cards
principle: The seam between two sections stops being a straight line: under the scroll it sinks in the middle into a pocket, funnel or notch while a loose scatter of word cards or chips lying on the upper section is carried into slots inside that pocket, so the edge itself collects what the section was about before the next ground takes over.
freshTake: For a library or archive service: the seam between a flat accent band and the ink band below starts as a straight line and, over about one screen of scroll, sinks in the middle into a square-bottomed pocket (a clip-path polygon whose two inner corners are scrubbed downward). Ten large word cards (book titles set in the display face, no icons) lie scattered and tilted across the accent band; each owns a fixed slot in a neat vertical stack inside the pocket, and scroll progress carries each card from its scattered spot to its slot in its own staggered window, straightening its tilt as it lands. Everything is scrubbed, so scrolling back scatters the cards exactly as they were. Flat colour, crisp corners, no shadows, no blur, no physics engine. On a phone use six cards and a narrower pocket so nothing covers the copy.
breaksWhen: On a phone twelve chips in a 390px column pile into overlapping rows over the headline and paragraph, so cut the count and the pocket width. Fewer than about eight objects look bare and the pocket reads as empty. Labels longer than two words make cards too wide to stack. Rebuilding a clip-path outline on every scroll frame of a very tall element can stutter on low-end phones. Reduced motion needs the cards already resting in the pocket.

name: Rack of sleeping devices wakes as the camera pulls back and one tap ripples through
principle: Under its heading the section opens on a close, nearly level crop of a row of dark devices. Once about two thirds of it is in view one timed camera move pulls back and tilts down to the whole rig while extra rows rise into place in a stagger; the front devices wake one after another and a scripted pointer acts on the first, the change spreads to the others, one of them disagrees and a single plain note names the finding, so the product's whole job is staged as a short film inside one frame.
freshTake: For a localisation tool: open close and low on one corner of a flat product window built in HTML, the other four of a row of five identical windows (one per market) cropped out of frame. When the block is mostly in view the camera cranes up and tilts down over about 1.2 s until all five lie on the ground plane at a high three-quarter view, and they wake one after another. A pointer edits one string in the first window, the change lands in the next three in turn in the one accent, and the fifth keeps the old wording and gets one plain note naming the mismatch. Flat planes with hairline ink edges, real text on them, no device mockups, glow or glass.
breaksWhen: Needs preserve-3d through several nested layers, and text on rotated planes can blur. It is time-based and plays once the scene is about two thirds in view, so a fast scroller passes the sleeping state and a visitor landing with it already in view gets the finished frame (so is the reduced-motion version). One fit factor scales the whole stage to the window height, so it gets small on short windows and phones, where background rows must go. Fewer than four foreground objects leaves the shelf empty.

name: Scroll is the input of a formula or a history, cut at its turning points
principle: A pinned run treats the scroll as the one input of a real relationship or record (speed, wind, price, dose, or the years of a history) and drives several outputs from it at once (a large readout, a chart that grows in steps, the picture of the current state), with the run divided in proportion to the real data rather than by eye and one event firing exactly at each regime change or milestone, so the length of the scroll is the argument, a story with a surprising shape is lived through rather than read, and scrolling back unwinds it.
freshTake: For a pension provider on a pale ground: the scroll is years of saving, 0 to 40, and one huge plain numeral is the pot computed every frame from the real compound formula with a fixed monthly deposit, with two smaller figures under it splitting it into money paid in and growth earned. Cut the pin by the model, not by eye, and at the exact year when a year's growth first exceeds a year's deposits fire one event once: the growth figure turns the accent in one hard step and the line under the numeral changes from 'what you put in' to 'what it earns'. Scrolling back unwinds it without the flourish. No dial, rings, drawn chart, gradients or shadows.
breaksWhen: Needs a relationship with one clean input and a formula that can be computed each frame; if the model is vague the scrub is decoration. Anchor jumps skip the story, short screens lose the pin, and reduced-motion visitors should get only the final frame with the numbers stated. Thin one-pixel lines on dark are fragile. The pin length should come from the model's own shares, not be set by eye. A history needs a surprising shape (a long flat stretch, one jump, a fall): a steady rise makes the chart pointless, and with fewer than five milestones the readout hardly turns.

name: Full-bleed opening picture closes into one shaped window
principle: The full-bleed picture or film that opens the page closes in from its own edges under the scroll, its clip losing its corners or insetting on every side, until it is one smaller window of a new shape standing alone on the page's flat ground while the type that lay over it falls away, so the first picture becomes an object on the page that then does a single job: it keeps playing, flicks through a short stack, takes a second picture behind its subject, opens again as the next state of the same place, or is buried by the next section rising over it.
freshTake: For a ceramics studio: open on full-bleed footage of the wheel with the studio's name set large along the bottom in one line. Over about half a screen of scroll the footage's clip-path closes from the full rectangle into a tall arch about 40 percent of the screen height wide, centred on a plain paper ground and still playing, while the name sinks away; build the arch as a polygon with the same number of points as the starting rectangle (a point at the middle of every edge) so the two morph instead of jumping, and let the footage shrink less than the window so the arch crops tighter rather than showing a miniature. The arch then holds for one screen beside a single line of copy and becomes the first picture of the section below instead of scrolling off, and the small nav mark appears only once the big name has gone. One ground, one ink, no gradient frame, glow, shadow or device mock-up.
breaksWhen: The two clip polygons must share the same number of points or the shape jumps instead of morphing. The subject must sit near the middle, because the picture has to read when cropped to the smaller window. On a phone the window is nearly as wide as the screen, so the end scale needs retuning and a portrait crop supplied. A heavy full-bleed video repaints the clip every frame and a 100-still frame sequence delays the first view; use one film or still. A second picture behind the subject must match its light, a before-and-after pair must register exactly, and a flick-through stack must stay close in tone or it reads as a slideshow. Packed into 150 px of scroll a flick skips the whole close, so give it at least half a screen.

name: The same job runs two ways on one clock
principle: The same job is run two ways side by side on one shared clock (the new way and the old, the product and the workaround, the flight and the drive), each playing its own flow, line or filling field while a large elapsed figure under it counts, so the fast one lands first with a small jolt and stops its figure while the slow one stalls through its steps and is struck through still counting; where there are several real jobs, a short list of them doubles as the control and each choice re-runs the race with its own pair of numbers, so the advantage is felt as time instead of claimed in copy.
freshTake: For a fibre-broadband provider on a pale ground: each row of a plain list is a real task (a 4K film, a game update, a year of photos) and is also the control. Beside it stand two square fields of small cells, one per line, that fill with ink cell by cell at each line's real speed, so the fibre field is full while the copper field is a third done. Two large plain numerals count the times; the fast one lands with a small spring and turns the accent, and a single rule strikes through the slow one while it keeps counting. Picking the next row clears both fields and re-runs the race with that task's numbers. Three rows, no map, no globe, no dials, no glow. On a software page the two fields become two flat panels of the same task: the old spreadsheet-and-email chase stalling on 'waiting for reply' beside the product's own flow, rebuilt from live parts, finishing in one step, each with its elapsed figure frozen at its foot.
breaksWhen: It plays on its own clock, so a visitor who scrolls past in a few seconds misses the slow half; start it when the section is mostly in view and let the list re-run it. It needs two real durations for the same job per row; invented numbers make it a gimmick, and more than four rows crowd the control. Two very close end points collapse on a map, and long place or task names run off a phone, so stack the two lines above the list there. The struck-through figure must keep its contrast. Reduced motion shows the finished state with both figures and the strike. Both sides must be truthful flows or durations; below about 700 px two panels must stack, and the new way should finish within about ten seconds.
